Issued at 148 PM CDT Thu Oct 22 2026

TONIGHT:

High pressure continues to depart to the east as surface low 
pressure approaches from the west. Low stratus and fog over 
western Lake Superior is expected to advance inland once again 
tonight. Areas near the Twin Ports, along the North Shore, 
portions of the South Shore, and the St. Louis River Valley have
the best chance of dense fog tonight. Areas farther inland 
including the Iron Range and Brainerd Lakes may see fog develop 
as well provided skies become clear and winds become calm. The 
tightening pressure gradient as low pressure approaches may keep
the winds high enough to provide a shallow mixed boundary layer
through the night. A few of the high-res models point to a few 
sprinkles over north-central Minnesota tonight in response to 
isentropic lift and a strengthening 850 mb LLJ.

FRIDAY:

A subtle warm front is expected to lift northeastward across 
the region Friday and Friday evening. Isentropic lift associated
with the boundary will lead to some scattered showers over 
central and north-central Minnesota. Models indicate weak 
instability generally less than 100 J/kg will develop in the 
warm sector through the afternoon. There appears to be 
sufficient vertical motion and instability to support occasional
lightning with the showers. I am hesitant to call them 
thunderstorms, per se. Rain amounts during the day and evening 
will be meager, less than a tenth of an inch. Showers along and 
near the warm front will lift into northwest Ontario overnight 
while convergence near the 850 mb LLJ ahead of the cool front 
will increase. It seems the shower chances will dwindle over the
Arrowhead of Minnesota while persisting over central and north-
central Minnesota. Highs on Friday will top out 15-25 degrees 
above normal with readings in the low to middle 70s. Areas which
see fog and low stratus in the morning will likely be cooler, 
as will areas along the North Shore where highs will be in the 
60s to low 70s.

SATURDAY:

By Saturday the mature low pressure system propagate eastward 
across the northern Canadian Prairies and into far northern 
Ontario. It's associated cold front will be cruising east across
the Northland providing another dose of light rain chances and 
perhaps a rumble of thunder across the region. MUCAPE increases 
a bit along the boundary as upper-levels cool and mid-level 
lapse rates increase to 7C/km. This could lead to some isolated 
storms at times but not expecting anything severe. Rain chances 
will quickly taper off west to east through Saturday night as 
the boundary moves into central WI. Additionally, out ahead of 
this boundary through the day the strong southerly flow will 
lead to widespread 70s, our last day of 15-25 degrees above 
normal for a while.

SUNDAY THRU NEXT THURSDAY:

A return to more seasonable temperatures as surface high 
pressure settles in behind the exiting cold front. Highs will be
in the 40s and 50s with overnight lows dropping below freezing.
The work week could see another uptick in rain chances but 
confidence remains low at this juncture. The 12Z suite of 
guidance suggests a pair of upper-level lows could impact the 
region as early as Sunday night. The first low of concern is 
ejecting eastward out of the central Rockies but will have to 
fight through the dry and cool air mass over the Northland. The 
overall trend has been shifting this system further south over 
the past several runs with only the Brainerd Lakes eastward into
NW WI now seeing a 20-40% chance of rain Monday.

The second upper-level system seems to hang back over the 
Canadian Prairies until midweek. A weak shortwave trough may 
propagate eastward over the Northland from that system Monday 
night and Tuesday which extends small rain chances north to the 
Canadian Border. The closed low itself will scoot eastward into 
northwest Ontario by early Wednesday morning providing a more 
widespread chance of light rain to the Northland. Temperatures 
aloft may be cool enough for a few "conversational" snowflakes 
to appear north of US-2 in Minnesota. Accumulation is not 
expected from any flurries at this time.
